strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful bottleneck in learned program verification: converting verbose solver outputs into effective supervision for small models. On 123 hard instances, Qwen3-4B improves correctness from 22.8% to 44.4%, acceleration rate from 11.1% to 24.7%, and end-to-end portfolio time from 185.7s to 165.7s (Table 3). These are meaningful improvements within the evaluated setting.

Soundness: Verifying both candidate validity and the original assertion under the candidate is a sensible safeguard against errors introduced by LLM rewriting or cast removal. Conditional on the sound verification oracle, this supports the safety of the resulting verification conclusions without requiring semantic equivalence between original and rewritten predicates.

Originality: The main contribution is an empirical data-curation approach combining normalization, semantic rewriting, augmentation, and verifier filtering. Table 4 provides useful evidence that the complete pipeline outperforms training directly on raw solver outputs for the 4B and 8B models.

Presentation and reproducibility: The running examples, staged pipeline, pseudocode, full prompts, training hyperparameters, verifier configuration, and hardware details make the approach reasonably accessible. Reporting three-run variability, inference-inclusive timing, and resolved baseline timeouts is valuable. The conclusion acknowledges the single-verifier scope, and there are no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness of the empirical explanation: The ablations do not isolate why V2 helps. Moving from V1 to V2 simultaneously changes target expressions, adds up to four teacher-generated candidates, and filters for correctness and sufficiency. Dataset sizes and matched training budgets for V0/V1 are not reported. A filtering-only baseline, size-matched comparison, and verified teacher-generation baseline without reference invariants are needed to distinguish compactness-driven learning from selection, augmentation, and distillation. The central claim that data quality rather than model scale is the primary limitation is therefore stronger than the evidence.

Formal precision: Sections 3 and 3.2 equate validity of V(A, P, I) with inductiveness. Checking an assertion on executions reachable from the program's preconditions establishes a reachable-state invariant; it does not establish consecution from every state satisfying I. Likewise, V(A ∪ {I}, P, q) checks the augmented whole program rather than the local implication I ∧ ¬B ⇒ q. The decomposition can still be sound, but the claimed guarantees should be stated accurately. Definition 4.2 also leaves V1 = UNKNOWN uncovered, whereas Algorithm 1 assigns it grade 0.

Practical acceleration is incompletely established. VBP is a useful idealized portfolio metric, but the claim of a 'zero-risk augmentation' assumes sufficient resources to run the baseline, two verification queries, and model inference without contention. The paper does not report an actual concurrent portfolio measurement or a resource-matched comparison. VBPE2E lacks an explicit formula, and frontier-model serving conditions and latency measurement details are missing. These omissions particularly affect the claim of practical parity with GPT-5.2.

Evaluation scope and uncertainty: Results cover one verifier, one benchmark source, and three sizes from one model family. Expanding programs into loop-level instances introduces dependence, but no program-level uncertainty analysis is provided. It is also unclear whether the three runs include independent fine-tuning seeds. The 0.6B model does not improve correctness, and its VBP changes only from 174.4s at V1 to 174.0s at V2, so claims of significant benefits across all scales are overstated. A focused benchmark is legitimate, but these results do not establish broad generalization.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite substantial implementation detail. Section 1 announces released code, models, and datasets without providing usable repository or collection addresses in the manuscript. The simplification threshold η, V0/V1 dataset statistics, teacher sampling configuration, and exact frontier-model inference settings are absent. The 80/20 split is described in samples rather than program groups, leaving unclear whether alternative invariants for the same program cross training and validation boundaries; training–evaluation overlap checks are also not documented.

Presentation contains consequential numerical and interpretive errors. Section 6 describes the 8B speedup rate as increasing from 8.5% to 10.7%, but those values are mean speedup factors; Table 3 gives rates of 10.8% and 21.7%. Its claim of 12–20 seconds of VBP reduction across all models excludes the 0.6B improvement of 8.9 seconds. The conclusion about extended reasoning is unsupported by an experiment described as using non-thinking mode for all models.

strengths: Significance: Curating solver-generated supervision is a useful contribution to neural program verification. Table 3 shows substantial improvements for Qwen3-4B: correctness increases from 22.8% to 44.4%, acceleration frequency from 11.1% to 24.7%, and end-to-end portfolio time decreases from 185.7s to 165.7s. The 8B results support the usefulness of the complete pipeline.

Soundness: Verifying both candidate validity and the assertion under the candidate assumption provides a sound basis for accepting rewritten training targets, conditional on the verification oracle. The method appropriately rechecks transformations that can change semantics, including cast removal.

Originality: The contribution is primarily an empirical understanding of supervision quality rather than a new verification algorithm. The V0/V1/V2 comparisons offer useful evidence that improving output syntax alone does not deliver the gains achieved by the full curation pipeline.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides clear examples, explicit grading algorithms, prompts, training hyperparameters, sampling settings, verifier configuration, and hardware details. Reporting three evaluation runs, latency-inclusive results, and baseline timeouts improves transparency. The acknowledged difficulty of resolving timeouts is appropriate, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central empirical explanation: Table 4 does not isolate simplification from verification filtering, augmentation, or supervision supplied by Kimi K2 Thinking. V2 changes all these factors simultaneously, while V0/V1 dataset sizes and matched training budgets are not reported. Filtering-only and size-matched controls, plus verified teacher-generated invariants without a reference invariant, are needed to substantiate the claim that compactness and removal of solver artifacts explain the gains. The broader claim that data quality is the primary limitation rather than scale remains unsupported.

Formal precision: Sections 3–4 equate validity on reachable executions, established by V(A,P,I), with inductiveness. These are different: a reachable-state invariant need not be preserved from every state satisfying I. Likewise, verifying the original program with an added assumption does not establish the standalone Hoare sufficiency condition introduced in Section 3. The composed verification procedure can remain sound, but the claimed inductiveness guarantees should be weakened or supported by explicit initiation and consecution checks.

Runtime interpretation: VBP is a useful portfolio statistic, but describing the augmentation as 'zero-risk' overlooks additional verifier processes, GPU resources, and contention. The manuscript does not establish performance under a matched resource budget. The exact latency-inclusive formula and frontier-model serving configurations are also unclear. Consequently, near-equality in average portfolio time supports a narrower claim than matching general model utility: the 4B model still trails GPT-5.2 substantially in correctness and acceleration frequency.

Reproducibility and evaluation scope: The manuscript states that code, datasets, and models are released but supplies no identifiable repository or collection URLs. The simplification threshold, teacher sampling configuration, V0/V1 dataset statistics, and program-level splitting/deduplication procedure are missing. Evaluation uses 123 loop-expanded instances from one benchmark and one verifier; related loops are not independent programs, and uncertainty across training seeds is not established.

Presentation and calibration: Section 6 mistakenly reports the 8B mean speedup factors, 8.5× and 10.7×, as speedup percentages; Table 3 gives 10.8% and 21.7%. The claim of 12–20 seconds of VBP improvement 'in all cases' also excludes the 0.6B model's 8.9-second improvement. Its correctness does not improve, and its V1/V2 portfolio times are nearly identical. These results warrant more qualified statements about consistent, significant gains across scales.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful bottleneck: converting verbose solver-generated invariants into effective supervision for small models. Table 3 shows substantial gains for Qwen3-4B, with correctness increasing from 22.8% to 44.4%, acceleration rate from 11.1% to 24.7%, and end-to-end virtual-best time decreasing from 185.7s to 165.7s.

Soundness: Accepting rewritten candidates only after correctness and sufficiency verification is a strong design choice. Conditional on a sound backend, semantic rewriting and potentially unsafe cast removal do not compromise the accepted verification conclusions.

Originality: The contribution is primarily an empirical insight and practical curation pipeline, rather than a new invariant-synthesis algorithm. Table 4 provides useful evidence that normalized solver outputs alone are less effective than the complete pipeline for the 4B and 8B models.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline is understandable, with concrete examples, pseudocode, prompts, training hyperparameters, sampling settings, and verifier configuration. Reporting three evaluation runs and an inference-inclusive timing metric strengthens the evaluation.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges the difficulty of resolving baseline timeouts and identifies evaluation with additional verifiers as future work. The application is constructive, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central explanation is insufficiently isolated experimentally. V2 simultaneously changes invariant representation, filters for correctness and sufficiency, and augments examples using Kimi K2 Thinking. Table 4 does not include equally filtered V0/V1 datasets, matched training sizes, or verified teacher-generated invariants without a solver reference. Consequently, it establishes a benefit from the combined pipeline but does not establish that compactness or semantic simplification drives that benefit, or that data quality is the primary limitation rather than teacher supervision and selection.

Important reproducibility and generalization details are missing. The manuscript reports 7,283 V2 samples but not comparable V0/V1 sizes, unique program counts, the simplification threshold η, or curation acceptance rates. The 80/20 split is described in samples without specifying whether variants of the same program remain grouped. Although training and evaluation use InvBench collections, overlap and near-duplicate checks are not documented. The claimed GitHub and Hugging Face releases also lack usable addresses in the supplied manuscript.

The practical speed claims require tighter qualification. VBP is a useful idealized portfolio metric, but taking the minimum of separately measured runtimes does not demonstrate a resource-controlled concurrent deployment. The 'zero-risk augmentation' claim overlooks additional CPU, memory, GPU, and contention costs. The exact end-to-end timing formula and large-model serving settings are unspecified, limiting interpretation of the close comparison between 165.7s for the 4B model and 163.4s for GPT-5.2.

The evidence has limited breadth and uncertainty characterization: one verifier, one benchmark source, and 123 loop-level hard instances derived from fewer programs. Three evaluation runs do not establish robustness across training seeds or program families. Improvements are also uneven: the 0.6B model's correctness does not improve, and its V1-to-V2 VBP change is only 0.4s. These results warrant narrower wording than consistent significant gains across scales.

Formal and numerical presentation needs correction. V(A,P,I) establishes that I holds on reachable executions; it does not generally establish consecution from every state satisfying I, despite the repeated identification with inductiveness. This does not invalidate the decomposition's safety argument, but it overstates the guarantee. Definition 4.2 omits the V1=UNKNOWN case, which Algorithm 1 handles. Section 6 also misreports the 8B speedup rates as 8.5%→10.7%, confusing mean speedup factors with the actual 10.8%→21.7% rates.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: converting verbose solver-generated invariants into training targets that help small models accelerate verification. Table 3 shows substantial improvements across several model families; Qwen3-4B improves correctness from 22.8% to 44.4% and reduces portfolio end-to-end time from 185.7 to 165.7 seconds.

Soundness: Rechecking rewritten candidates for correctness and sufficiency provides a sound safeguard against erroneous LLM transformations, assuming the verification oracle is sound. The paper appropriately distinguishes invariant correctness from verification speedup.

Originality: The main contribution is a useful data-curation approach combining normalization, semantic rewriting, augmentation, and verifier filtering. The cross-family results provide evidence that training-target representation matters beyond a single model.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline, examples, metric definitions, prompts, algorithms, training hyperparameters, and verifier configuration are generally clear. Three-run results and explicit reporting of unresolved timeouts are helpful. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on one verifier; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness of the empirical attribution: The V0→V1→V2 ablation changes representation, filtering, data quantity, and supervision from a strong teacher simultaneously. V2 expands 4,000 raw invariants into 7,284 retained samples, but comparable retained counts and matched training budgets for V0/V1 are not reported. Without size-matched ablations, filtering-only controls, and verified teacher generation without reference invariants, the results do not establish that semantic simplification or compactness is the decisive mechanism.

Formal precision: Sections 3.1–3.2 equate reachable-state validity with inductiveness. Checking V(A,P,I) establishes that I holds on executions from the original preconditions; it does not establish the consecution obligation from every state satisfying I. Similarly, V(A∪{I},P,q) can exploit the original program semantics rather than proving the textbook invariant sufficiency condition. The resulting verification procedure can remain sound, but the claimed guarantees of inductive invariant synthesis require correction or explicit initiation/consecution checks.

Timing evidence and reproducibility: The headline frontier-model comparison uses a virtual portfolio minimum rather than a demonstrated deployed portfolio. It needs clearer accounting for concurrent resource contention, additional verifier processes, inference serving configuration, and latency measurement for the large/API models. Appendix G lists one L40S but does not explain how all large baselines were served. Matching GPT-5.2 on this metric also coexists with substantially lower correctness and speedup rates, so the comparison should remain narrowly qualified.

Dataset separation: Appendix D describes splitting the augmented rows 80/20 without specifying grouping by source program or loop. Multiple rewrites of the same input could therefore cross training and validation partitions. The manuscript also lacks an explicit overlap or near-duplicate audit between the inherited training programs and InvBench. These are unresolved evaluation risks, rather than evidence that test leakage occurred.

Reproducibility and statistical scope: The abstract promises public GitHub code, but the manuscript supplies no repository address. Teacher decoding settings, V0/V1 dataset construction details, and whether the three runs include independent training seeds are unclear. The hard evaluation comprises only 72 programs expanded into 123 correlated loop instances; program-level uncertainty estimates would strengthen the timing comparisons.

Claim calibration: Table 4 shows lower VBP after raw-data fine-tuning for every listed family, despite mixed syntax and correctness effects. The narrative that raw fine-tuning fails to improve challenging verification is therefore too broad. Likewise, accepting grade-2 samples guarantees neither speedup nor compactness; 'provable quality guarantees' should identify precisely which properties are certified.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: making solver-generated invariants better training targets for small models. Table 3 shows substantial improvements across several model families. For example, Qwen3-4B correctness rises from 22.8% to 44.4%, while portfolio end-to-end time falls from 185.7 to 165.7 seconds.

Soundness: Rechecking rewritten predicates against the original program is an appropriate safeguard for both LLM rewriting and potentially unsound cast removal. Assuming a sound verification oracle, the two-query decomposition supports sound verification outcomes without trusting the language model.

Originality: The contribution is primarily an empirical data-curation insight rather than a new verification algorithm. Combining normalization, semantic rewriting, augmentation, and verifier filtering is a useful extension of the prior one-shot training framework. The V0/V1/V2 comparisons provide evidence that the full pipeline improves on raw-target training.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally clear, with concrete examples, explicit metrics, prompts, algorithms, training hyperparameters, and verifier configuration. Reporting correctness separately from speedup is particularly helpful. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on one solver and limited progress on timeouts; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central empirical interpretation: The ablations do not isolate improved target quality from augmentation, filtering, and additional training exposure. V2 expands 4,000 source invariants into 7,284 retained examples, but matched-size or matched-update comparisons are absent, and V0/V1 dataset sizes and filtering are insufficiently documented. A verifier-filtered raw-data baseline, one-rewrite-per-program comparison, and direct teacher-generation baseline would help establish whether semantic simplification is the decisive ingredient rather than more data or teacher distillation.

Formal claims: Section 3 equates holding on all reachable executions with inductiveness, but V(A,P,I) establishes the former. It does not establish consecution from every state satisfying I. The decomposition can remain sound, but the claimed inductive-invariant guarantees and interpretation of Rcorrect are stronger than the implemented checks justify. Similarly, Proposition 4.3 guarantees correctness and sufficiency, not compactness or acceleration: grade-2 examples explicitly need not speed up verification.

Timing evidence and reproducibility: The headline frontier-model comparisons depend on a virtual portfolio metric and model latency. The manuscript does not adequately specify serving hardware, inference configuration, or latency measurement for the large and proprietary baselines; the single-L40S hardware description does not explain their deployment. Nor does it establish measured concurrent-portfolio performance under resource contention. The reported 162.9 versus 163.4 seconds supports similar observed portfolio means, but not a general efficiency equivalence, especially given the 14B model's 43.4% correctness versus GPT-5.2's 72.4%. 'Without test-time compute overhead' also needs qualification because the portfolio uses generation and additional verification queries.

Evaluation scope and uncertainty: The hard evaluation contains only 72 distinct programs expanded into 123 correlated loop instances. Three-run standard deviations do not establish uncertainty across programs, and it is unclear whether runs include independent fine-tuning seeds. Some incremental gains are small relative to variability—for example, Llama-3.1 V1 versus V2 end-to-end time is 170.4 versus 169.2 seconds. Program-level paired uncertainty estimates and another benchmark or verifier would strengthen the generalization claims.

Data and artifact reproducibility: The 80/20 split is described over augmented samples without stating whether all rewrites of a source program remain together, leaving possible train-validation overlap unresolved. Appendix D also reports retaining 187 grade-1 candidates although Algorithm 2 returns only grades at least 2; subsequent filtering may protect the final dataset, but the accounting needs reconciliation. Finally, the abstract claims public GitHub code, yet the supplied manuscript provides no identifiable repository URL.

strengths: Significance: WONDA provides a useful practical contribution to learning-assisted verification. On the hard split, Qwen3-4B correctness increases from 22.8% to 44.4%, while end-to-end portfolio time decreases from 185.7 s to 165.7 s. Improvements across Qwen3, Llama, and Mistral make the evidence stronger than a single-model demonstration.

Soundness: Rechecking rewritten candidates for correctness and sufficiency is a sensible safeguard against unsound LLM transformations and cast removal. Under the stated sound-oracle assumption, the verification decomposition supports sound program-verification outcomes.

Originality: The contribution is primarily empirical and methodological: converting verbose solver proofs into compact training targets, augmenting them, and filtering them by verification outcomes. Although the ingredients are established, their combination and the observed transfer across model families offer useful new evidence.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful examples, explicit metrics, stagewise ablations, three-run results, and detailed prompts, training settings, and verifier configuration. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on one verifier. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The ablations do not isolate the proposed explanation for the improvements. V2 simultaneously changes target representation, adds multiple candidates, and filters for correctness and sufficiency; it grows from 4,000 raw invariants to 7,284 samples before the train/validation split. Matched-data and matched-training-budget controls, filtering-only experiments, and verified teacher generation without reference invariants would distinguish semantic simplification from augmentation, selection, and distillation.

The formal exposition conflates reachable-state invariance with inductiveness. V(A,P,I)=TRUE establishes that I holds on executions of P, but does not establish preservation from every state satisfying I. Likewise, V(A∪{I},P,q) retains the program and is not the standalone Hoare-style sufficiency condition introduced in Section 3. These checks can support sound verification while failing to establish the stronger inductive-invariant claims.

The headline frontier-model timing comparison needs qualification. VBPE2E is a virtual portfolio metric with baseline fallback and additional parallel verification resources. The manuscript does not adequately specify inference deployment, latency measurement, or reasoning settings for the large and proprietary baselines. Qwen3-14B-V2 and GPT-5.2 have similar mean portfolio times, but substantially different correctness rates (43.4% versus 72.4%); the evidence supports similarity on this metric, not general capability parity or an unqualified absence of test-time compute overhead.

The narrative overstates the failure of raw-data fine-tuning. Table 4 shows that V0 improves mean end-to-end portfolio time over the base model for every listed family and size, and improves correctness for Qwen3-4B/8B and Llama-3.1-8B. Syntax degradation is supported, but the claim that only the full pipeline delivers meaningful verification improvements is too strong.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The abstract claims public GitHub code, but the manuscript provides no repository address. V0/V1 dataset sizes and treatment of overlength targets are unspecified, and the 80/20 split does not clarify whether augmented variants of the same program are grouped. Program-level separation and overlap checks should be documented, alongside whether the three runs vary training seeds or only inference.

Evaluation breadth and uncertainty limit the conclusions. The hard split contains 123 loop instances from only 72 programs, so observations are correlated. Program-level confidence intervals and broader verifier or benchmark coverage would strengthen generalization claims. These limitations do not erase the consistent practical gains, but they support a weak acceptance rather than a stronger recommendation.
